title_original: ‘Who asked that? You should be ashamed of yourself!’: Judi Dench answers questions from Ian McKellen, Lorraine Kelly, David Hare and more
excerpt_original: Fans and famous friends put their nosiest questions to the 91-year-old actor It’s mid-afternoon and Judi Dench and I are sitting in the “den” of her country house in Surrey. It’s one of the smallest rooms in her Elizabethan home: timber beams, terracotta-painted walls, her…

blocks.text: I t’s mid-afternoon and Judi Dench and I are sitting in the “den” of her country house in Surrey. It’s one of the smallest rooms in her Elizabethan home: timber beams, terracotta-painted walls, her father’s consulting-room desk and chair within touching distance, together with the bronze “Dr Dench” plaque that used to hang on the railings outside their family home in York.

Behind Judi’s head hangs an enormous painting of her as M, presented as a gift on her last day of filming on Skyfall . Through the latticed windows is a view on to the garden, which is crowded with trees she plants for lost friends and family – a beloved oak, a tribute to her late husband, actor Michael Williams, towers above the pond. Even though the room is suffused with autumn sunshine, all the lights are on in the house. Judi has always needed light around her – she’s been afraid of the dark since she was small.

I am with the 91-year-old Oscar-winner – one of Britain’s finest Shakespearean actors, the first female M in the James Bond franchise and a national treasure (a term she loathes) – to put questions to her from friends and fans. It’s taken me an hour to get her into this room: a lot of coaxing and cajoling, the promise of a game of Bananagrams once we’ve finished; it’s like bribing a seven-year-old to do their homework. It was the same when we worked on her memoir, Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? Just as I was about to press record before beginning my questions, she’d decide the foxes needed feeding or the candles had to be lit. And I’ve lost count of the number of times I had to sit and wait while she fashioned the red wax of a Babybel into comedy lips, or challenged herself to see how much toffee popcorn she could cram into her mouth.

links.text: Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?

blocks.alt: A head and shoulders shot of Judi Dench gazing thoughtfully to her right, with her left hand touching her chin, wearing a deep-purple dress against a taupe background
blocks.caption: Photograph: Nick Knight/trunkarchive.com

blocks.text: Deflecting and mucking about is Judi’s modus operandi. It’s not an end in itself – it’s her process, and it’s also how she works as an actor. Games help to bond a company and build relationships. But for Judi they serve an additional purpose – they are a necessary step towards accessing something deeper, more profound within herself. She describes it as taking the froth off the beer in order to reach what’s beneath. Eventually, today, we get stuck into our Q&A – and things are just as lively as in the run-up.

What is the worst thing your parrot, Sweetie, has said to you and who trained her to say bizarro things? Suzy Eddie Izzard , comedian and actor She’s never said anything particularly rude to me, but she once said to my cleaner, Barbara, who’s been with us for 40 years: “You’re a slag.” She also said to my nephew: “Drop your trousers.” You have to keep your wits about you because you never know who she’s going to offend next. I have no idea where she gets it from. Certainly not from me – I’m too busy trying to teach her Shakespeare.

blocks.alt: Judi Dench offers a treat through the bars of a cage to Sweetie
blocks.caption: Judi Dench with her cheeky pet parrot, Sweetie. Photograph: BBC

blocks.text: Is there anything you did in your younger days that would make you wince now? Kate, Warrington Where do I start? I was quite a tearaway as a child and often getting into trouble – whether it was for posting a rat through a neighbour’s letterbox, firing dried peas at my father’s patients as they waited outside the surgery, or throwing a slipper over a bannister at my boarding school and having it land on the headmistress’s supper tray as she was coming up the stairs. I also wince when I think of the behaviour that caused my mother to say, “You are, without doubt, the most intolerant person I’ve ever met.”

What is the thing you have done in your life that you are most ashamed of? Henry, London One of the worst is losing Byron’s tiepin. The memory still brings me out in a cold sweat. When Michael and I were living in Stratford-upon-Avon, our great friend John Carroll was about to open an exhibition in Hall’s Croft. He invited us along one evening and handed me this beautiful object, saying, “This is Byron’s tiepin.” Then he and Michael wandered off, and it slipped out of my hand and disappeared down a crack between the floorboards. I was too frightened to own up. Not good, is it?

Was there a moment when you thought , “I can make a living as an actor. It could be a full-time job ”? Emlyn, Devon My very first job out of drama school was as Ophelia at the Old Vic. My performance was savaged by the critics, but instead of terminating my contract, Michael Benthall, who ran the Vic at the time, decided to keep me on. Over the next four years, he kept renewing my contract. He made me believe I could have a career as an actor.

blocks.alt: Judi Dench gestures expressively on stage
blocks.caption: Dench at a dress rehearsal of Hamlet at the Old Vic theatre, London, in 1957, where she was making her London debut as Ophelia. Photograph: Bob Haswell/Getty Images

blocks.text: If you had not become an actor, what would you have liked to be? Sharleen Spiteri , Texas singer-songwriter When I was very small, I wanted to be a ballerina. I was always working up routines with my friend Ann Parsons and arranging the chairs and getting my family in to watch. Then when I was a teenager, I set my heart on becoming a theatre designer. I even went to art school. After seeing the design for the RSC’s King Lear in 1953, I realised I’d never be as inventive as that and so chose a different career path.

Graham Norton once said you lied like a rug when you claimed you hadn’t been to a nightclub. What else have you lied about? Jill, Northern Ireland My age, I should think, continually. And occasionally my height. I also managed to convince a lot of people that Wellington Arch, that wonderful monument by Hyde Park Corner, had been turned into a Tesco for the royal family.

Out of all the characters you’ve played, which one reflects you as a person? Lethal Bizzle , rapper I hope it’s not Lady Macbeth. That question is tricky to answer since I’m not looking at myself from the outside. All I’ll say is you learn something new about yourself in every part. And also, as actors, we’re always drawing on our own lives to create the character.

blocks.alt: A black and white photograph of the pair standing close, gazing intensely
blocks.caption: Dench as Lady Macbeth with Ian McKellen (Macbeth) at the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1976. Photograph: Donald Cooper/Alamy

blocks.text: What were the challenges you faced being the first female M in the Bond movies? Angela, south- west France I put myself under a lot of pressure because I didn’t want to let the side down. I remember the terror of that first day on GoldenEye. Although I’d worked a lot in theatre and had done quite a bit of TV, I’d only made a handful of films – none of them big-budget blockbusters – so I felt a huge responsibility, and I also had to follow in the footsteps of Bernard Lee.

blocks.alt: Judi Dench, in white blouse, wears a grey jacket and a red scarf, and poses holding a red folder
blocks.caption: As M in GoldenEye, 1995. Photograph: Keith Hamshere/Getty Images

blocks.text: What is your favourite memory from the Bond set? Lily, Liverpool I associate all of them with different standout moments: the thrill and utter terror of turning up for my first day as M on GoldenEye; flying in a glass‑bottomed helicopter with Colin Salmon while filming The World Is Not Enough and swooping down over Swindon. And then there was the night in Skyfall (which happened to be my birthday) when Daniel Craig drove me through the streets of London in the Aston Martin and all the traffic lights turned green for us.

blocks.alt: The pair stand on a misty Scottish hillside road next to a vintage car
blocks.caption: With Daniel Craig in Skyfall, 2012. Photograph: François Duhamel/Columbia Pictures/ Eon/Danjaq/Allstar

blocks.text: Shag, marry, kill: Daniel Craig, Pierce Brosnan , Sean Connery ? Helen, London Who asked that? You should be ashamed of yourself, Helen from London. I can’t possibly answer that.

Do you find theatre or big Hollywood films more fulfilling? Why? Jonathan, Peterborough Oh, theatre is much more fulfilling. It’s different every night, and always a work in progress. If you’re not happy with something, you have the chance to make it better the following day. But with filming, once you’ve finished it’s up there for everyone to see and you can’t change it. Whenever I watch myself on screen I think about all the choices I thought about making and probably should have done.

How do you feel at the end of a theatre performance when it all just goes wonderfully well; the audience “gets it” and you’ve given everything? What’s it like to take those curtain calls? Lorraine Kelly , broadcaster My overwhelming feeling at a curtain call is relief. I’m thinking, “Gosh, I got through it, and hopefully got away with it.” One of my most difficult curtain calls was during Antony and Cleopatra. After I died at the end, Miranda Foster, who played Charmian, had to take the live snake from my hand and pop him into a sack behind my throne. But on this one particular night the snake escaped. As I was being carried up the aisle by the four soldiers, I could hear this hissing sound. I then had to rush round the back of the auditorium, through a pass door and into the wings. As I ran on to take my bow, I saw the snake come out of the side of my wig. He obviously wanted to share the curtain call. I was so traumatised that I lost my voice for two days.

blocks.alt: The female characters grieve over Mark Antony’s body on a bier
blocks.caption: As Cleopatra (above) with Anthony Hopkins (Mark Antony), Miranda Foster (Charmian) and Helen Fitzgerald (Iras) in Antony and Cleopatra at the National Theatre in 1987  and with her husband, Michael Williams, in Mr and Mrs Nobody (right) at the Garrick theatre, London, 1986. Photographs: Donald Cooper/ Alamy; Alastair Muir/Rex

blocks.alt: Michael Williams and Judi Dench in Victorian costume sit in deckchairs onstage

blocks.text: Are there any particular actors you always corpse with or are tempted to corpse with? What’s been your worst episode of corpsing? Stephen Fry , writer, actor and broadcaster How long have I got? I’ve worked with so many actors who’ve made me corpse – Billy Connolly, Alec McCowen, [my husband] Michael … especially during Mr and Mrs Nobody when his moustache fell off.

One of the worst episodes of corpsing was during a television production of Ibsen’s Ghosts. It was directed by Elijah Moshinsky and he added a scene where we had to eat a meal in silence – all very sombre – Ken[neth Branagh], Mike Gambon, Freddie Jones and me. And Natasha Richardson had to walk around the table, dishing out potatoes. When she reached Mike Gambon, he casually said – and it’s not a particularly funny line out of context – but under his breath he said, “Just the usual eight.” I am afraid Ken and I were uncontrollable … You know when you laugh so much it causes you pain? We were completely gone. Eventually over the intercom came a voice that said, “Mr Branagh, Miss Dench, you may leave the studio.” I think we bonded over that.

What do you do if you forget your lines on stage , or if your fellow actors forget their s? Tim, Queensland, Australia All you can do is hope that the other actor prompts you – and vice versa. The worst is drying in a musical. In a play you can improvise your way out of it, but if you’re in the middle of a song and forget the words, the music carries on. I remember one night a group of friends came to see me in Cabaret. I was so keen to impress them that I completely forgot the words – that’s what fright does to you!

What drew you to the major motion picture Cats (2019) ? And do you regret appearing in it? Bertie, Norwich What drew me to the film was unfinished business. I was meant to be in the original stage production in 1982, but had to withdraw shortly before it opened because I snapped my achilles tendon. And, no, I don’t regret appearing in it. How lucky to be asked. And whatever the merits of the final film, I made some good friends.

blocks.alt: Judi Dench in cat-like fur and ears
blocks.caption: Dench as Old Deuteronomy in Cats, 2019. Photograph: Universal Pictures/Working Title Films/ Amblin Entertainment/Allstar

blocks.text: Wh ich is your favourite of the places you’ve travelled to for work and why? Phoebe, Luton I’ll never forget the first time I toured America. It was 1958 and on my travels I was lucky enough to see many of the jazz greats live in concert: Count Basie at Birdland, Billie Holiday in San Francisco. I even had the chance to meet Miles Davis on several occasions. Heady days.

Very high up on that list would be India. That’s where we made The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel. I had to return to film the sequel to make sure I hadn’t dreamed it. My daughter, Finty, maintains it’s become my spiritual home and I think she might be right.

When you were shooting The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel, what did you wear on your head when you used to swim around the moat to visit Dame Mags [Maggie Smith] at the hotel in Udaipur ? Celia Imrie , actor We were all staying in this beautiful hotel in Udaipur. Each room had steps down into a pool that ran around the circumference. One day, I was swimming around the hotel, on my way to meet Mags, who was lying on a sunbed. As she saw me approach she shouted, “Oh Jude, go and get the Bananagram!” And so I swam back, climbed the steps to my room and tied the Bananagram to my head with a belt. How else could I prevent it from getting wet? I couldn’t hold it aloft and swim with one arm or I’d still be there, going round in circles.

blocks.alt: The cast stand on a porch, smiling and clapping towards a cheering crowd
blocks.caption: As Evelyn Greenslade (centre) with Celia Imrie, Ronald Pickup, Diana Hardcastle, Maggie Smith and Bill Nighy in a scene from The Second Best Exotic Marigold Hotel, 2015. Photograph: Fox Searchlight/Allstar

blocks.text: Did you get the shits while filming it? Chris, Buckinghamshire I expected a higher standard of question from a Guardian reader – especially from Buckinghamshire. But since you’re asking, Chris, no, I didn’t.

Have you ever had a supernatural experience? Natasha, Newcastle Yes, the first time I went to Scotland. Michael, Finty and I had been invited to stay at the actor Robert Urquhart’s house. As we were driving along the coast approaching Ullapool, Michael said, “I have no idea how we’re going to find this place. We’ll have to ask.” I said, “I know exactly where it is. There’ll be a war memorial, we turn right, and two roads up on the left we’ll turn in and it’ll be on the right-hand side.” And that’s exactly where it was. What’s odd is I’d never been there before, I’d never seen an image, there was no map, we weren’t given directions … just the address.
I’ve also seen a ghost at the Haymarket theatre during Michael Denison’s memorial service, but that’s for another day …

My mother has macular degeneration, like you . What can I do to help, without reducing her independence? Phil, Yorkshire The most helpful thing you can do is to be there for her – either in person, or at the end of a phone. If your ma’s at home, she’ll probably feel safer because she’ll know her way around the house. But if she’s in an unfamiliar environment … that can sometimes be disorientating. If you’re out and about, paint a picture for her. Rather than say, “There’s a lovely house over there”, describe the colour of the door and the way the roof slopes down. You now have to be her eyes.
Are there benefits to being 90 -plus? Judi, Dorset None whatsoever. Next question.

What’s the secret to longevity? Gemma, Buckinghamshire Mainly luck, I’d say. You also need opportunities, a loving family and good friends. Laughter is vital – at least it is for me – as well as remaining optimistic; always look for the pluses in life.

Would you ever have a facelift like Kris Jenner ? Emma, Buckinghamshire It’s too late for me to have a facelift now; the whole thing has dropped off. But, whoever Kris Jenner is, good luck to her, I say.
What tree would you most like planted in remembrance of yourself? Annette, Somerset Something frightfully tall and willowy, a reminder to people of what I looked like.

What is the best piece of advice you have been offered as a gardener? Flinders, Australia I’d never consider myself a gardener. I know my plants and trees, and I’m lucky to have a fantastic gardener, Joe, who looks after them all. But I could never be an actual gardener because I’m too frightened of worms – ever since a worm jumped into my sandal when I was four.

Has the Birnam Wood tree we planted in your garden survived the dry summer? Ian McKellen , actor It has indeed survived, and it’s grown a few inches since you last saw it. I’ve been watching it very carefully, especially during the recent storms. I’m also keeping an eye on Antoninus, which is a sapling taken from the Sycamore Gap seedlings. They’re very near to each other in the meadow, almost within talking distance.

blocks.alt: A tree-lined path forms a leafy tunnel in Birnam Wood, with walkers ahead
blocks.caption: A tree that started life in Birnam Wood, Perthshire, is flourishing in Dench’s garden. Photograph: Marco Secchi/Alamy

blocks.text: You’re a massive Everton fan. Have you visited the new stadium yet? Jeff, Liverpool No, not yet. Maybe one day, who knows? I can no longer see very well, so I wouldn’t know who was playing or where the ball was.

What period of history would you most like to have lived in if the 20th century was unavailable? Henry, London Of course, I would have liked to be around in Shakespeare’s London to see the plays at the Globe, or, alternatively, in 18th-century Venice on the off‑chance of bumping into Canaletto.

Apart from Shakespeare, who is your favourite poet? Any particular poem? Tim, Littleport That’s very difficult. I grew up surrounded by poetry. My father could recite the whole of Hiawatha [Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s epic poem The Song of Hiawatha], as well as The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam. I don’t have a favourite poet, but WB Yeats would be very high up on the list. A particular favourite is The Lake Isle of Innisfree.

You have Irish heritage. Do you embrace it or do you consider yourself English through and through? Christopher, Arkansas I definitely embrace my Irish heritage – as I do my Dorset heritage because that’s where my father came from – and I was born and grew up in Yorkshire. And I recently found out I have Danish ancestors. You embrace everything that you’re made of, don’t you? It defines who you are.

What is one part you yearned for but were never asked to perform? Alan Titchmarsh, broadcaster I wanted to be in Edward Albee’s Three Tall Women, but for some unknown reason they wouldn’t consider me. When it was announced that Maggie Smith had been cast in the West End premiere, I sent her a note saying: “Couldn’t it be called ‘Two Tall Women and One Much Shorter One’?”

blocks.alt: The three actors stand on stage during a performance
blocks.caption: Anastasia Hille, Frances de la Tour and Maggie Smith in Three Tall Women in 1994 (above), and Dench as Titania (right) with Paul Rogers as Bottom and director Peter Hall during the filming of A Midsummer Night’s Dream, 1968. Photographs: Donald Cooper/ Alamy; David Farrell/Getty Images

blocks.alt: A black and white photograph of the actors and directors

blocks.text: How did you and your fellow cast members stay positive making Peter Hall’s Midsummer Night’s Dream in what looks like a freezing, muddy, wet wood ? Phil, Bristol When you’re young, nothing fazes you – not even the inclement British weather. I remember filming it in Compton Verney, which is in the middle of the Warwickshire countryside. There were no showers, and so at the end of each day I’d have to travel back to my cottage in Ettington in all my makeup. I was wearing my own clothes – trousers and a polo-neck sweater – but I still had green hands and a green face. On one occasion, a workman caught sight of me walking up the lane and fell off his ladder.

Is it true that in the 1976 King Lear at the Royal Shakespeare Company , you laughed every night so uncontrollably at the gouging -out of Gloucester’s eyes that you had to withdraw from the production? David Hare , writer and director Please, Mr Hare, you know me better than that. What happened was this … John Woodvine was playing my husband, and one night we were pulling out Tony Church’s eyes – the way you do when somebody pops round to your house for a visit – and after the line, “Out, vile jelly!”, John would fling the sticky eyeball over his shoulder and into the wings. Anyway, after we’d been performing the play for several weeks, I just happened to glance up, and saw that there were about five eyes stuck to the proscenium arch. Stage management hadn’t removed them. When Trevor Nunn [the director] found out, he told us off because he knew it made us laugh. John wasn’t allowed to throw them after that. I didn’t withdraw from the production. My contract ended and I chose not to extend it for the London transfer.

What is your first thought in the morning and your last thought at night? Catherine, Plymouth First thought in the morning: Oh, what a relief … I made it. Last thought at night: How lucky to have a bed for the night, and a roof over my head. Bless Andy Burnham for trying to end rough sleeping by Christmas.

National treasures have been doing well on Celebrity Traitors – are you tempted to give it a go, and would you make a good traitor? Helen, London I’d like to think I’d make an excellent traitor, and I love the idea of wearing a hooded cloak. Could they make one short enough? I met James Blunt [who appeared on Celebrity Traitors] on The Graham Norton Show last week. What a charming, beautiful man.
What is the meaning of life? Celeste, Hong Kong Oh stop, I can’t possibly answer that because I have no idea how to begin. Sorry, Celeste from Hong Kong – if ever you find out, please let me know.
